1.explanation: The core of the problem is in src/languages/kotlin.js: the syntax‐highlighter’s “class” mode is defined with end:/[:\{(]|$/ and excludeEnd:true, which makes the mode terminate before hitting the brace when there’s a colon (inheritance) in the declaration. As a result, that brace is not part of the class‐scoped highlighting and picks up a different color. To fix this, the ‘end’ regex for the class rule must be adjusted (for example, removing ‘\{’ from the end pattern or changing how inheritance colons are handled) so that the opening brace remains inside the same highlight scope.
1.bug_scenario: The screenshot shows a Kotlin code snippet in a syntax‐highlighted editor (VSCode/JSFiddle) where the opening brace “{” after an inherited class declaration (e.g. class TABLE: Tag { ) is rendered in a different color than other class/body braces. In other words, the highlighter’s Kotlin “class” rule is stopping at the colon and not including the brace in the same scope, so that brace falls back to a different (punctuation) style.

2.explanation: The bug lives in the Kotlin highlighter definition in src/languages/kotlin.js—the anonymous default-export function that defines the grammar. In its “class” rule it uses end: /[:\{(]|$/ and excludeEnd: true. By including “{” in the end pattern, the opening brace is excluded from the class context and thus is not scoped together with its matching brace. This split breaks bracket-matching and results in differently colored braces. Adjusting this end regex (for example, removing “\{” so the rule doesn’t terminate on the brace) will keep the brace inside the class scope and restore uniform bracket coloring.
2.bug_scenario: In the Kotlin snippet shown in the screenshot, the class declarations that inherit from another type (for example, “class TABLE: Tag { … }”) have their opening and closing braces highlighted in a different color from each other. In other words, because the syntax highlighter’s “class” rule ends on the colon (and even on an opening brace), the brace tokens fall outside of the class-decl context and are tokenized (and colored) independently, causing the brace pair to no longer be recognized and colored as matching brackets.
